newsitem.title: USA: BOXING-LEWIS AND AKINWANDE TRY TO RESTORE HEAVYWEIGHT ORDER.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-LEWIS AND AKINWANDE TRY TO RESTORE HEAVYWEIGHT ORDER.

text.p: The first step in restoring some semblance of order in the ring to a heavyweight division rocked by the Mike Tyson affair takes place Saturday when World Boxing Council champion Lennox Lewis meets unbeaten fellow-Briton Henry Akinwande.

The 12-round title fight is being touted as "Tall Order," a reference to the stature of both Lewis and Akinwande, who are 6-foot-5 (1.96 m) and 6-foot-6 1/2 (1.99 m), respectively, and the fact that the site is at an elevation of 7,000 feet (2,133 m).

"Basically, I can't wait to get in there and prove my stuff to Henry Akinwande," the 31-year-old Lewis, who has a record of 30-1 with 25 wins within the distance, said at the final pre-fight news conference on Thursday.
"I also want to prove to the American public what I can do."
Akinwande, 32-0-1, said he was prepared for whatever strategy Lewis might try.

"My first plan is to jab and work from there," Akinwande said. "My second plan is to fight him. It just depends how he comes out. It doesn't make any difference to me. I'm going to do what I have to do. Whatever it takes, I'll find a way to win."
Promoter Dan Duva boasted that the winner of the all British clash would eventually unify the heavyweight division.

Duva said he anticipated Saturday's winner would meet the victor of a bout between World Boxing Association champion Evander Holyfield and International Boxing Federation title holder Michael Moorer, tentatively set for November.
Neither Lewis nor Akinwande, however, cared to look that far ahead.
"Unification? We'll wait and see," said Lewis.
Said Akinwande, "I'm not looking past Saturday. I'm just looking forward to being the WBC champion of the world. My mind is on Lennox Lewis."

In the past Akinwande has depended on his long, stiff left jab, which he often follows with a good, but not spectacular, combination right. Those in the Lewis camp are not convinced Akinwande's arsenal is enough to upset the champion, who is listed as an 8-5 favourite.
"He's got some skill and some speed," said Lewis's manager, Frank Maloney. "But Lennox has the same skills along with more power."
Lewis's promoter, Panos Eliades, added: "Akinwande's a fine boxer, but I don't know what he's doing fighting Lennox Lewis."
Don Turner, trainer of both Akinwande and Holyfield, dismissed all that talk.
"Frank Maloney doesn't fight," Turner said. "He doesn't know a left hook from a fish hook."
